author: Colorado Wealth Management Fund
title: How To Retire Today: Dividends
text:
This research report was produced by The REIT Forum with assistance from Big Dog Investments .
Lately, I’ve been hearing from investors about the importance of total return.
More specifically, I’ve been hearing about how total return doesn’t matter.
This is a tricky subject because there are very important factors to consider on each side.
When should investors not worry about total return? Investors shouldn’t be worried about watching total return on their position over the next few hours or the next few days.
Source: Google images
If they feel compelled to check their accounts daily, they are speculating rather than investing.
When an investor buys a very high credit quality bond and intends to hold it until maturity, they shouldn’t be concerned with the total return in the meantime. Often, bonds will trade on dealer markets that are less favorable to retail investors than the broader stock markets. To be clear, I’m saying dealer markets are worse for investors than the broad market is for investors.
If the investor buys into an index fund shortly before it drops by a couple percentage points, they shouldn’t sweat it unless they intended to trade the position actively. The REIT indexes, like the Vanguard Real Estate ETF ( VNQ ), iShares U.S. Real Estate ETF ( IYR ) and the Schwab U.S. REIT ETF ( SCHH ), will correlate heavily with interest rates in the short term. However, over the longer term, the equity REITs have regularly performed well even during times of rising rates. Investors shouldn’t overemphasize the first few days or weeks of an investment.
When the investor is buying a relatively illiquid stock, they should not concern themselves with the variance in the closing price. When the liquidity is poor, we will often see securities stuck within a range. The price could easily swing by a few percentage points each day without breaking its regular range. Unless the investor is trying to create a short-term trade on the illiquidity, it makes sense to ignore the small fluctuations.
When does total return matter? Total return is absolutely critical in a few situations:
When the investor is performing short-term trades to capitalize on mispricing, the total return is critical. In these situations, there is often some illiquidity in the market, so the total return only really matters on the day the investor closes the position.
Total return matters a great deal when the dividend is reduced. I have seen too many examples where investors have earned 50% on an investment over several years while the price declined by 50%. I know of another investment that is guaranteed to produce returns that are at least that good. It is called a savings account. It comes with FDIC (Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation) insurance. An investor who is simply referring to withdrawals from their savings account as income would’ve had similar total returns. That doesn’t mean investors should be constantly focusing on the price movement, but when a price decline is matched with dividend cuts it usually indicates that the investors’ entire thesis was wrong.
Total return is of paramount importance in situations such as RAIT Financial Trust (RAS) or Wheeler ( WHLR ). Both of those garbage REITs have chopped the dividend to zero. Dividend investors who previously refused to care about total return will find that their income from the position has been chopped to zero. If they still care about having income, they will need alternative places to invest that capital. Depending on how terrible of a price they initially paid, they may have witnessed around 98% of their investment being destroyed.
Simply holding onto the stocks does not prevent the loss. Neither is likely to ever pay another common dividend. There will be no more income for the shareholders.
The importance of dividend growth At The REIT Forum, we focus on REITs with solid dividend growth in addition to a healthy yield. The emphasis on growth is important. Dividends are rarely cut shortly after being raised. A REIT that is continually growing their dividend and growing their earnings is in a much better position.
Some investors criticized my decision to buy Simon Property Group ( SPG ) instead of WHLR. I purchased shares in August of 2017. They argued that their double-digit yield was dramatically better than my 5% yield.
They felt that even with my dividend growth I would not match their yield on cost for a decade or more.
Source: Seeking Alpha
Their yield on cost is now 0%. Simon Property Group continues to give me raises. Since purchasing SPG, my position is up 5.41%. While the returns haven’t been significant, it was a lot better than purchasing WHLR.
When an investor is buying a security for long-term income generation and growth, they don’t want to be too obsessed with short-term movements. A dip in the share price is an opportunity to buy more. A decline of 60% from the initial entry price is not an opportunity to buy more. It is a sign from the market that the analysis was incorrect.
When the equity REIT indexes plunged in early 2018, many investors told me they couldn’t buy REITs in this environment. Many were avoiding the sector precisely as it hit bottom. Since then, the indexes have rebounded nicely. I’ve been buying new positions throughout the year. Most of those positions currently carry significant unrealized gains. Perhaps, more importantly, the lower prices I acquired by buying during periods of fear have enabled me to acquire great companies at very good prices.
During that period of fear, the yields were elevated.
Today, there are still several great dividend growers available. Some of the great stocks have already recovered, while others remain on sale.
By focusing on the fundamentals of the company, I have been able to avoid sucker yields and acquire several great REITs. For instance, Equity Residential ( EQR ) is up significantly since my purchase. They have also been raising the dividend.
That dividend growth is backed by growth in earnings and revenues. It is reinforced by an A- rated balance sheet.
Source: EQR investor presentation
Why is this so important for retirees to understand? I have heard from countless retirees who are stuck in a terrible position. They needed a very high dividend yield to meet their living expenses. They bought into very high yield stocks with the expectation that they could ignore share price movements. Since then, they’ve seen the price decline and the dividends decline.
It is critical for these investors to value dividend safety above other metrics. The price movements aren’t too important unless the dividend is reduced. When the dividend goes down instead of up, the price movements become critically important.
This is especially important for retirees because they often have a smaller margin for error. A younger investor can learn this lesson the hard way and cut back on expenses or work additional hours to recover their losses.
It is a painful lesson, but they can still recover. Dividend cuts for a retiree can decimate their lifestyle. For evidence, simply look at the comment stream following articles on failing dividend payers.
Perhaps, I should refer to them as former dividend payers since the dividend has passed away.
I want to focus on helping readers avoid those situations. There is no need to gamble on the highest yields. There are several great dividend growth stocks available.
